rationale: Jeremiah is a prophet opposed by his own town and his own family. The people of Anathoth, his hometown (Jeremiah 1:1), say, "You must not prophesy in the name of the LORD, or you will die by our hand" (Jeremiah 11:21, BSB), and he is told, "Even your brothers— your own father's household— even they have betrayed you" (12:6). Matthew 13:57 pairs the same two circles, "his hometown" and "his own household." The Pulpit Commentary on 13:57 suggests the link, tentatively: "Possibly Jeremiah's experience (Jeremiah 11:21; Jeremiah 12:6) gave rise to this proverb." The type is motif, a recurring picture of the rejected prophet, because Matthew neither cites nor names Jeremiah here, and the two passages share almost no wording. The label is plausible, not strong, for two reasons. The suggestion comes from one commentator who calls it possible. And the Expositor's Greek Testament calls the saying a proverb "not Jewish merely, but common property of mankind," with Greek and Roman parallels, so it may need no single Old Testament source.
